cards.a: SDN separates the control plane from the data plane, centralizing the network brain in a controller. Northbound APIs talk to apps and southbound protocols (NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow) program devices, making network services programmable and centrally managed.

cards.q: Why does SDN matter for modern networks?
cards.a: It is the foundation of DNA Center, SD-Access, and VXLAN/LISP, turning the network into an API-managed service with programmability, rapid change, template-based automation, consistency, analytics visibility, and policy-driven security.

cards.q: Where does the control plane live in SDN compared to the data plane?
cards.a: The control plane is centralized in the controller, while the data plane stays on the switches/routers. Management sits at the orchestration layer and service/application logic rides on apps and APIs.

cards.q: What are the five layers of the SDN architecture?
cards.a: Application (business apps), Northbound API (app to controller), Controller (control logic), Southbound API (controller to device), and Infrastructure (hardware).

cards.q: What is the difference between the northbound and southbound API?
cards.a: Northbound = up to applications; southbound = down to devices. The controller sits between them in the SDN stack.

cards.q: Which southbound protocols does modern SDN favor?
cards.a: NETCONF (YANG + XML), RESTCONF (YANG + REST), and OpenFlow (flow table), while CLI/SNMP are the legacy options. Modern SDN favors NETCONF/RESTCONF over YANG.

cards.q: What is the difference between controller-based and model-based SDN?
cards.a: Controller-based SDN centralizes control logic in a controller; model-based SDN uses YANG data models. Overlays (VXLAN/LISP) are a third approach, and Cisco's enterprise version combines controller (DNA Center) with SD-Access.

cards.q: What are the main benefits of SDN?
cards.a: Agility (rapid change), automation (template-based), consistency (single source of truth), visibility (analytics), and security (policy-driven).

cards.q: What are the trade-offs or concerns with SDN?
cards.a: The controller is a single point of failure unless made highly available (HA), devices must support the protocols, new skills are required, and migration is best done through a hybrid path with gateways for legacy devices.

cards.q: Which commands enable and verify YANG/NETCONF support on a device?
cards.a: Configure netconf-yang or restconf globally, then verify with show platform software yang, show netconf-yang sessions, and show running-config.

cards.q: How do you troubleshoot a config that fails over the API?
cards.a: If no config applies, check whether the protocol is enabled (netconf-yang). Authentication failure points to credentials/API, session drops to transport (check netconf sessions), a missing model to YANG, and a down controller to HA failover.

cards.q: What is the modern southbound replacement for CLI/SNMP?
cards.a: NETCONF/RESTCONF combined with YANG data models are the modern southbound protocols; CLI/SNMP are considered legacy.

cards.q: Why must an SDN controller never be a single point of failure?
cards.a: Because the controller is the centralized brain; if it goes down without HA, the whole network loses central control, so controllers must be deployed with high availability (failover).

cards.q: What is Cisco's enterprise implementation of SDN?
cards.a: Cisco SDN = DNA Center + SD-Access, which uses an overlay of VXLAN and LISP on top of the fabric.
